summary: FireSense is a web platform for tracking wildfires worldwide and alerting people who could be affected. We use NASA FIRMS (VIIRS NOAA-20 near-real-time satellite data) to get fresh fire hotspots. A user picks locations of interest on an interactive map, registers, and receives an email when a fire is detected within about 2 degrees of their location. We also trained a machine-learning model (Random Forest) that estimates fire detection confidence from weather conditions such as temperature, pressure and wind. These values come from the Open-Meteo API. FireSense addresses the challenge by turning open NASA data into personal, timely warnings, not just a map for experts. This matters because wildfires are growing more frequent and severe, and early notification gives people time to evacuate and helps communities allocate resources.
details:
What it does and how it works. FireSense has three parts: a React web app, an ASP.NET Core backend and a Python ML module.

  • Frontend: a one-page parallax site that explains why fire tracking matters and which factors make fires worse (heat, wind, dry soil). It has a Google Maps view with place search (Places Autocomplete) and click-to-add location markers. A “Get notified” modal registers the user with their username, email, password and chosen coordinates.
  • Backend: a REST API with registration and login (JWT), subscription management (add, list, delete locations), and an endpoint that returns current fires. Every 10 minutes, a background service pulls new fire hotspots from the NASA FIRMS API, compares them with every subscriber’s locations, and sends an email through SMTP (MailKit) if a fire is nearby. Data is stored in SQL Server, and the service is deployed on Azure.
  • ML module: a Random Forest classifier trained on historical fire detections matched with weather data. It takes weather features (temperature, sea-level and surface pressure, wind speed, wind direction at 10 m and 100 m, gusts) for given coordinates and time, and predicts a confidence class from 0 to 100 in steps of 25. Weather data comes from Open-Meteo (forecast or archive, depending on the timestamp). We tuned hyperparameters with GridSearchCV and 5-fold cross-validation (best: 300 trees, max depth 10).

Benefits and intended impact. Users get personal alerts for places they care about, such as home, family or farmland, without watching a map. Early warnings support faster evacuation and let people coordinate with authorities. The global coverage fits the fact that wildfires cross borders. Combining satellite detections with weather-based prediction is a step from reacting to fires toward anticipating where conditions favor them.

Tools and technologies.

  • Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, SCSS, react-spring (parallax), Google Maps JavaScript API, axios.
  • Backend: C# / .NET 6, ASP.NET Core Web API, Entity Framework Core + SQL Server, AutoMapper, CsvHelper, JWT authentication, MailKit/MimeKit, Swagger, Azure.
  • Data / ML: Python, pandas, scikit-learn, Google Colab, NASA FIRMS API, Open-Meteo API.

Creativity. We combine three open data sources (NASA satellites, weather data, Google Maps) into one consumer-friendly service. The scrolling interface with a dark map theme makes a heavy topic easy to approach. Applying ML to fire detection confidence from weather alone is an unusual angle.

Factors we considered. We chose NRT satellite data for freshness, a 10-minute polling interval to respect API limits, and email as the simplest channel that works anywhere. We also weighed privacy and security (hashed passwords, JWT). The ML module is an early prototype with room to grow.
